sources.headline: Nationwide ground stop could cost US airlines hundreds of millions
sources.text: Airline executives support modernising FAA systems as US Transportation Secretary Duffy seeks $50bn from Congress for FAA overhaul.Following the nationwide ground stop last week, United States airlines could face a financial hit of hundreds of millions of dollars even as airline executives press for increased investment in ageing air traffic control infrastructure.The four largest US airlines – American Airlines, Delta Air Lines, United Airlines and Southwest Airlines – could face a combined hit of $345m to pretax earnings, according to brokerage firm Bernstein.Recommended Stories list of 3 itemslist 1 of 3Trump denies responsibility for FAA nationwide ground stoplist 2 of 3What forced the US to ground all planes? A router switch, we now knowlist 3 of 3After a nationwide ground stop, US faces aviation infrastructure questionsend of listThe effects of Friday’s ground stop continued to ripple through airline schedules on Monday, with more than 18,500 flights within, into or out of the US cancelled since the disruption began, according to FlightAware data.Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy told CNBC on Monday that the wider impact of the disruption could run into the “billions of dollars”. No official estimate of the total economic cost has been released yet.Flights were grounded across the country for more than four hours on Friday, and the disruption continued to affect airline schedules over the weekend.Delta Air Lines CEO Ed Bastian also said the financial impact could run into the “billions”, telling Fortune on Monday that the disruption underscored the need for greater investment in the country’s air traffic control infrastructure.Bastian pointed to the vast sums investors are putting into artificial intelligence and data centres, adding that the US should also be investing in its aviation system.“We can’t even get $50bn to fix our skies,” he said.United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby agreed that the disruption should be a “call to action”, saying the air traffic control system needed greater investment in modern technology to improve its reliability.Transportation Secretary Duffy has asked US Congress for $50bn for air traffic control and airport infrastructure upgrades, an addition to the $12.5bn lawmakers approved for air traffic control modernisation last year.The existing system relies on outdated equipment and needs a comprehensive overhaul, he said.But Democrats have questioned the request, saying only about $1bn of the $12.5bn already approved has been spent so far.On Sunday, US President Donald Trump called on Congress to approve the funding, arguing that the upgrades should be carried out all at once rather than in stages.“We have already started the work, but it should be done all at once, not in drips and drabs. Congress must approve,” Trump wrote on Truth Social.The funding debate is moving into a narrow window for congressional action. The House and Senate are scheduled to convene once more before the end of the year.Speaker Mike Johnson has said lawmakers will take up the administration’s funding request during the current Congress’s lame-duck session, but Democrats have demanded more information on how the money will be spent.The precise cause of Friday’s failure remains under investigation. Duffy has said the problem began at a remote Federal Aviation Administration (FAA) site in Arkansas where workers from defence contractor L3Harris were replacing ageing copper wiring with fibre-optic cables.The Government Accountability Office, the congressional watchdog, raised concerns about the FAA’s management of its modernisation programme in a September report. It found that the agency had not developed an integrated schedule for the first phase of upgrades, and warned that poor planning increased the risk of disrupting air traffic control operations.

Trump says he needs funding for air traffic control after ground stop

Issued on: 16/11/2026 - 23:01

US ​President ​Donald Trump, pressed on a ​technology ‌failure ⁠that ‌grounded thousands of ⁠flights last week, ​on ‌Monday told reporters ‌that ​the government needed funding for upgrade ​to ​air traffic ​control equipment. FRANCE 24's Monte Francis speaks with Sheldon Jacobson, Professor of Computer Science at the University of Illinois. He explains that "the Republicans have had full control of the House and the Senate since the President came in. They controlled everything. If they needed the money and wanted the money they could have approved the money. The fact that they didn't, in the the different bills that have been passed, suggests that it's more than just money that is going on here".

FAA Ground Stop Update, Democratic Leadership Contest, Trump's Travels To Asia

Transcript
Good morning. You're reading the Up First newsletter. Subscribe here to get it delivered to your inbox, and listen to the Up First podcast for all the news you need to start your day. Today's top stories Travelers are expected to face continued disruptions at airports as airlines recover from Friday's nationwide ground stop. As of Sunday evening, more than 2,300 flights have been canceled, and more than 8,000 flights within, into or out of the U.S. have been delayed, according to FlightAware.com. Dallas-Fort Worth and Atlanta airports saw the most disruptions, with over 250 delayed flights each. U.S. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said L3Harris Technologies Inc., a federal contractor, was doing routine maintenance in at least one remote location, changing copper wire to fiber optics.
Aircraft are seen at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport in Arlington, Va., Saturday, Nov. 14, 2026, after the Federal Aviation Administration grounded flights nationwide.
Tom Brenner/AP
hide caption
Tom Brenner/AP
🎧 The U.S. air traffic system remains safe, and this recent incident is considered an unusual meltdown, NPR's Joel Rose tells Up First. The Federal Aviation Administration believes it has identified the issue, and airlines will be ready for the holiday travel rush. Rose says the nation's air traffic system has suffered from decades of underinvestment by Congress and administrations from both parties. Before the ground stop, Duffy had requested $30 billion to upgrade the air traffic control system. Now he seems to be asking for $50 billion by the end of the year, on top of the $12.5 billion for air traffic equipment that the Trump administration secured from Congress last year. Democrats, who will control Congress in January, are not responding positively to Duffy's latest request. Rose expects Democrats to seek more clarity on the administration's spending and the causes of the ground stop.
As Democrats gear up for substantial majorities in Congress, one question looms: who will take the helm? So far, no one has challenged Rep. Hakeem Jeffries for the House speaker role. Meanwhile, Sen. Chris Van Hollen of Maryland is setting his sights on unseating longtime leader Chuck Schumer in the Senate. 🎧 A wave of incoming senators has spent months hearing voters demand change in Washington. NPR's Eric McDaniel says this presents a real opportunity for Van Hollen and a potential risk for Schumer, especially after the recent election results. Van Hollen needs 30 Democrats to secure a simple majority. He has support he needs from popular progressives like Bernie Sanders, and incoming members like Abdul El-Sayed and Peggy Flanagan, McDaniel says. Since votes are cast by secret ballot, it's uncertain how many will back each leader when they convene in a few weeks, and McDaniel says anything could happen. President Trump is traveling to the Philippines and China this morning for a high-profile trip, which includes a trilateral summit with Chinese President Xi Jinping and Russian President Vladimir Putin. This marks Trump's second visit to China this year. The trip to Asia comes as the administration faces scrutiny following Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's resignation. Huang admitted to an extramarital affair with a woman linked to China's top spy agency, according to The New York Times. He traveled to China with Trump earlier this year; this time, tech billionaire Elon Musk is accompanying Trump to Shenzhen.
🎧 It's not unusual for presidents who face midterm election defeats to shift their focus to foreign policy, NPR's Mara Liasson says. But Trump's recent foreign policy efforts, including tariffs and the war in Iran, have been widely unpopular and seen as reasons why his party lost in the midterms, Liasson says. The White House said that Trump isn't expected to address pressing issues like the war in Ukraine or tensions with China during this trip. Instead, he plans to discuss the war in Iran and nuclear weapons. Trump will also skip mentioning Huang's affair. Bringing up the Nvidia situation could serve as a reminder that many in Congress believe the U.S. should restrict access to advanced chips in China. Trump disagrees with Congress on the matter, likely due to his ties with Huang, who committed millions of dollars for Trump's ballroom, Liasson says. Living better
Woman with insomnia
Mono/Getty Images
hide caption
Mono/Getty Images
Living Better is a special series about what it takes to stay healthy in America. Sleep plays a crucial role in weight management. Studies have found that poor sleep can increase appetite and lead to overeating, making it harder to shed pounds. On the flip side, quality sleep might actually enhance your weight-loss efforts. One study found that participants in a year-long weight-loss program who enjoyed better sleep lost more weight and fat. So, prioritizing sleep could be your secret weapon in the journey to a healthy weight. Here's what researchers say: 😴 While evidence linking more sleep to weight loss is limited, there is consistent science connecting insufficient sleep to weight gain.😴 Lack of sleep increases activity in brain regions associated with pleasure and reward, making it harder to make good food choices.😴 Not having enough sleep can disrupt circadian rhythms and reduce insulin sensitivity, encouraging fat storage and weight gain.😴 The relationship between sleep and food goes both ways. Eating added sugars and saturated fats disrupts sleep and reduces deep sleep, while consuming fruits, vegetables and fiber improves sleep quality and decreases nighttime awakenings.
Picture show
A "Route 66" sign is painted on the asphalt near Amboy in the Mojave Desert in California on Feb. 27, 2019.
Eric Baradat/AFP via Getty Images
hide caption
Eric Baradat/AFP via Getty Images
Route 66 is celebrating an incredible century as America's most iconic highway. Stretching across eight states — from the vibrant streets of Chicago to the sun-soaked shores of Santa Monica, Calif. — this legendary route invites you to embrace the spirit of adventure on the open road. Imagine cruising through vast plains, rolling prairies, stunning canyons and shimmering deserts. Along the way, you'll discover a mix of big cities, charming cow towns and ghost towns. Over the decades, Route 66 has inspired countless songs, been captured in books, been seen in artwork and been celebrated in Pixar's 2006 animated movie Cars. So hop in, buckle up and experience the magic of Route 66 through these photos. 3 things to know before you go

NASA's Voyager 1 has traveled farther than any human-launched object and is about to reach a new milestone: reaching a distance that's one light-day away from Earth.New Orleans port officials have filed a lawsuit against the owner and operator of the Atlantic Asphalt tanker that crashed into a docked cruise ship in the Mississippi River. They are seeking at least $1 million in damages.Mauricio Pochettino, who guided the U.S. men's national soccer team to a Round of 16 finish in the 2026 FIFA World Cup, is leaving to become the head coach of Manchester United in the English Premier League. sources.headline: US air travel largely returns to normal as funding fight brews
sources.text: WASHINGTON - US air travel largely returned to normal on Nov 16 after more than 18,000 flight cancellations over three days stemming from Nov 13’s longest ground stop in 25 years, suspected to have been caused by a single router installed during routine maintenance.Speaking on CNBC, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy estimated the economic impact of the disruptions – which also delayed nearly 28,000 flights – would be in the billions of dollars.As air travel stabilized, the conversation in Washington turned to how the air traffic control network will be fixed, how it will be funded and who was to blame for Nov 13’s alarming shutdown.By 1.30pm Eastern Time on Nov 16 (2.30am Singapore time on Nov 17) there were only 330 flight cancellations and 3,000 delays, down from more than 2,300 cancelled and 11,000 delayed on Nov 15, according to flight-tracking site FlightAware.US President Donald Trump said on Nov 16 that funding is needed to upgrade the system. “Essentially, what you saw was very old equipment that had a heart attack,” Trump told reporters.The four largest US airlines could face a US$345 million (S$444 million) earnings hit from the nationwide ground stop, brokerage Bernstein estimates.Duffy on Nov 13 upped his request for funding for air traffic control and airports to US$50 billion from US$30 billion.The FAA is still using ageing equipment including Compaq computers, floppy disks, 25-year-old obsolete routers and paper strips to track aircraft.“This rickety system is telegraphing to the American people, ‘hey, we need investment’,” Duffy said on Nov 16. “Now is the time to do a big dollar amount to modernise the system.”Republican Senator Eric Schmitt weighed in by saying the necessary funding was long overdue. “We should just go all in here and get this thing fixed,” Schmitt told Reuters. “The can has been kicked for a long time ... Clearly this is a decades-old problem in the making.”Democrats in Congress say Duffy has spent only US$1 billion of the initial US$12.5 billion approved in 2025 for air traffic control while USDOT says it finalised plans for much of the funding and needs more money for telecoms upgrades.They also want hearings into what led to the communications disruptions that brought nearly all US air travel to a halt for more than four hours on Nov 13.Duffy and Republicans want quick action on the additional funding in the final weeks before the current Congress goes home and Democrats take over in January. REUTERS

sources.headline: Thousands of US flights still cancelled or delayed two days after grounding of planes nationwide
sources.text: Flights across the US were returning to normal levels, after a weekend of disruption as the national air-traffic control system recovered from a technical failure that prompted a rare national ground stop.More than 2,500 flights into or out of the US were delayed and 325 flights cancelled on Monday morning, a significant drop from the thousands delayed and cancelled on Friday, according to the latest data from FlightAware., external"What you saw on Friday was very, very old equipment that had a heart attack," President Donald Trump said on Monday.Asked by reporters if he took any responsibility for the ground stop, Trump said he did not. "I don't take any responsibility," Trump said, praising his officials. "They did a great job, Secretary Duffy, acted incredibly.""The only responsibility should be, for 40 years they should have done this, with this system that is probably on average 50 years old," he said.Trump called on Congress to "give us the money" to fix the US' air traffic control systems.Every US airline was affected by Friday's ground stop, which lasted for more than four hours. The total number of flight cancellations had topped 17,000 by Sunday, according to Bloomberg, which cited aviation data providers.Thousands of other flights were delayed. The stoppage left passengers stuck inside planes on the tarmac, unable to take off or to return to their gates. Others were stranded in airports, sleeping on the floor and desperately trying to get in touch with their airline. The ground stop also had a knock-on effect on schedules around the world, with some flights out of the UK and Europe cancelled.Speaking on Sunday, Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said: "As we look to the end of the day and into tomorrow, we should be running at full capacity."Duffy told the BBC's US partner CBS News that the after-effects meant it would take time for things to return to normal. "We have airplanes and crews that are out of position, so it takes a little bit of time." In its update on Sunday evening, American Airlines also said: "We are set up for a good start to the week and do not anticipate additional broad cancellations related to this incredibly disruptive industry-wide event."Some other major US carriers gave updates of their own earlier the same day. Delta Air Lines said: "While most flights are operating normally, some customers may still experience delays or cancellations."Alaska Airlines said its operations, and those of Hawaiian Airlines, had "mostly recovered", though thousands of people were still trying to reach their destinations.The issue occurred during an attempt to update part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate.In the wake of the chaos, Duffy has issued calls for a wider upgrade of the technology, to the tune of tens of billions of dollars. He and Trump have urged Congress to approve more money for modernisation work to take place. Debate has turned to whether or not funds already approved by Congress are sufficient for the purpose.Duffy told CBS that Congress had been "very specific" about existing funding, which was "all spent". He added: "What I don't have money for is a new telecom system. I don't have money for new software." Speaking to the same network, Jim Himes, a congressman from the opposition Democratic Party, said: "This is not a Congress money problem." Instead, he argued, it was "a prioritisation problem".Investigators are still working to determine the root cause of the issue and who might have been at fault.In his account of what happened, Duffy said a computer router installed as part of an upgrade from copper wire to fibre started sending out faulty signals. The router - a piece of equipment which directs traffic across the network - was in El Dorado, Arkansas. The signals "flooded our network", he said. Duffy said that issues would continue to arise until the US made major modernising changes to its air control system. The system needs a complete overhaul, he said."Let's not lie to each other," he said on NBC's Meet The Press. "We have to make investments into a network that has been neglected for decades."Experts say the technology used by the US for flight communications is antiquated. Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described it as "a house that's about to be condemned".He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

Trump breaks silence on US ground stop, demands more money from Congress

President has been quiet on ground stop since it began on Friday, instead issuing statements on social media about other topics

Associated Press
Published: 11:00pm, 15 Nov 2026Updated: 12:26am, 16 Nov 2026

US President Donald Trump on Sunday broke his silence on the nationwide ground stop that snarled airline travel this weekend, using the incident to push Congress on money to fully upgrade America’s air traffic control system.

The Republican president has been conspicuously quiet on the ground stop since it began on Friday afternoon, instead issuing statements on social media about completely different topics as frustrated passengers were left stranded at airports and his government scrambled with airlines to restore normal travel.

Trump said in a new post on his social media platform that his administration has begun upgrading that system, but that the task should not be done in “drips and drabs”.
